sentences.text: Eodromaeus was an extinct genus of basal theropod dinosaurs, a name combining Greek words for 'dawn' and 'runner'.
This animal possessed a low, rectangular skull measuring roughly 12 centimeters in length.
Its cranium held fifteen sharp, knife-like teeth, while a separate row of tiny teeth lined the pterygoid bone on the palate.
The forelimbs were much shorter than the hindlimbs, ending in hands with five digits where the fourth and fifth fingers were notably slender and abbreviated.
This creature reached a total length of about 1.2 meters and weighed between 4.5 and 6.8 kilograms.
Paul Sereno estimated that Eodromaeus could run at speeds of about 32 kilometers per hour.
Fossils were first found in 1996 by paleontologist Ricardo N. Martinez and volunteer Jim Murphy, whose name was honored in the specific designation murphi.
The genus and its type species, E. murphi, were officially named in 2011 by a team including Martinez, Paul C. Sereno, and others.
As a basal carnivorous theropod, it likely hunted small prey using its sharp dentition.
Eodromaeus is classified within the order Saurischia and the suborder Theropoda, with Saurischia serving as its parent group.
When initially described in 2011, it was considered the earliest known member of the Theropoda.
These dinosaurs lived approximately 230 million years ago in the Carnian stage within the Ischigualasto Formation in northwestern Argentina.
All known specimens are found within the humid Scaphonyx-Exaeretodon-Herrerasaurus biozone of that formation.
A later study by Baron et al. (2017) placed Eodromaeus as a basal herrerasaurian and moved the family Herrerasauridae outside of Dinosauria.
